data.title: Watchdog: Zacharia's exit doesn't 'wipe clean' dispute over legal credentials
data.description:
A D.C.-based ethics watchdog group that accused Katie Zacharia of misrepresenting herself as a lawyer is urging the State Bar of California to press ahead with an investigation into her credentials after she was ousted as White House press secretary.  

The Campaign for Accountability, which filed a Bar complaint against Zacharia earlier this week, said her exit from the White House does not resolve allegations that she may have violated California law by portraying herself as a lawyer despite never being licensed to practice law.  

“The White House clearly recognized that keeping Katie Zacharia as Press Secretary was untenable given the facts that have come out about her conduct,” Michelle Kuppersmith, the group’s executive director, said in a Friday statement to The Hill.  

“Even so, her departure does not wipe clean the fact that she consistently, and apparently falsely, held herself out as a lawyer,” Kuppersmith added. “This is a crime in California, so we continue to urge the state’s Bar to investigate and impose any appropriate penalties.”  

The group filed its complaint on Wednesday, the day after Zacharia’s brief tenure got off to a rocky start with a shaky first press briefing and scrutiny into her professional history.  

Zacharia, a graduate of Pepperdine Law School, has often referred to herself in media appearances as a “lawyer” despite never having passed the bar exam. Her LinkedIn profile also referenced her role as “general counsel” for Fix California, a conservative nonprofit founded by Trump ally and former administration official Richard Grenell.  

She has claimed to have worked as an associate on the International Practice Team of Beijing-based Zhong Lun Law Firm, and President Trump described her as an “attorney” when he announced her as former Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt’s replacement.

When asked by reporters on the South Lawn this week which state she took the bar exam in, Zacharia replied, “When I moved to China.” She later said she misheard the question due to the noise of Marine One and assumed it was about where she went after law school.  

In subsequent interviews, she admitted she never passed the California bar exam, telling The New York Times the results were “somewhat inconsequential” since she was planning to move overseas at the time.

“It was never my intent to go into the practice of law,” Zacharia told Fox News’ Sean Hannity Thursday night. “When I went to go engage in media and give legal analysis, I consulted attorneys and legal professionals as to whether or not they agreed that I could be labeled a lawyer, both because I had a valid Juris Doctor from a good law school, a reputable law school, Pepperdine Law School, and in conjunction with the fact that I did have actual substantive legal experience.” 

The watchdog group alleges her use of the terms may have been unlawful because each representation “conveys to an ordinary listener that Ms. Zacharia is a licensed attorney entitled to practice law.” 

It is commonly believed the term “lawyer” refers to someone who has graduated from law school, while an “attorney” is someone who has passed the bar exam and is licensed to practice law in a specific jurisdiction. 

But the American Bar Association (ABA) makes no such distinction, using the titles interchangeably to describe any “licensed professional who advises and represents others in legal matters.” Many state licensing statutes, including California’s, don’t either.  

California law asserts that “no person shall practice law” in the state unless that person is “an active member of the State Bar” and makes it a misdemeanor offense to unlawfully portray oneself as “practicing or entitled to practice law.” 

It remains to be seen what outcome could come from the complaint, if the State Bar of California even chooses to pursue it at all. Data compiled by Vitreo, an independent hub for judicial data, shows that disciplinary agencies process tens of thousands of complaints each year, and the vast majority are dismissed, screened out or resolved privately.

Because Zacharia is not a member of the California Bar, the agency can’t take any professional disciplinary action against her even if it identifies wrongdoing. It could, however, refer her for prosecution on criminal charges.  

The White House confirmed Friday afternoon that Zacharia was “transitioning out” of the role just five days after President Trump announced her as his pick to fill the press secretary role.

data.title: Oil reaches $110 per barrel
data.description:

The Big Story 

Oil hits $110 per barrel for first time since May

An international oil benchmark hit $110 per barrel on Friday, as the industry faces persistent shocks from the U.S.-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars. 

© Kamran Jebreili, Associated Press file

The price of Brent crude oil, the international standard, hit $110 on the nose during Friday trading. That marked the first time it has reached that level since May 20, less than three months after the U.S. and Israel launched the Iran conflict. 

 

The commodity is trading at roughly $109.75 as of late Friday afternoon. 

 

Brent crude prices peaked in late April, when the benchmark topped $120 per barrel.  

 

Oil prices shot up during the early months of the conflict with Iran and sunk down below $80 per barrel throughout much of June and July — as the U.S. and Iran were operating under a ceasefire both sides accused the other of violating.  

 

But as the war, now approaching the eight-month mark, has persisted, oil prices have surpassed $100 yet again.  

 

West Texas Intermediate crude, the North American benchmark, also topped $100 per barrel on Friday for the first time since Sep. 21. 

 

The increase in oil prices has translated to higher prices at the pump for Americans. Regular gas in the U.S. costs about $4.33 per gallon on average, AAA reported Friday.  

 

Diesel also costs more than $6.30 on average, nearly $2.70 higher than a year ago, according to AAA.

data.title: Press secretary under Clinton says Zacharia was 'set up to fail'
data.description:
Katie Zacharia was set up to fail by the Whtie House and President Trump, who made her White House press secretary without preparing her, former Clinton-era White House Press Secretary Joe Lockhart said Friday.

“I don’t mean this to sound partisan or overly critical of the president, but she is, in fact a victim here,” Lockhart said during an appearance on CNN. “She was thrown out there in a place where she wasn’t prepared.”

Lockhart said when he got the job of press secretary, he took two months off to go to school, sit down with the national security team, budget team and essentially get prepared.

“I wasn’t going to go out, the president wasn’t going to let me go out, the staff wasn’t — until I was absolutely ready, and that’s when I went out,” he said. “She did this in a couple of hours. “

“She was set up to fail, and she has failed. But it shouldn’t be surprising,” he added. “There ought to be a little bit of sympathy here for her that she was not given the ability to succeed here.

Zacharia, who was appointed to the position a week ago, is “transitioning out” of her role after President Trump told reporters that he told her to “reconsider” the position, a White House official told The Hill.

She got off to a rocky start after facing scrutiny about her claims of being a lawyer as reports surfaced about her not being licensed to practice law in any U.S. state. A watchdog group called the Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the State Bar of California asking for an investigation into her claim.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Zacharia failed her California bar exam after she received her law degree from Pepperdine University. She said Thursday that the results of the test are “somewhat inconsequential.”

Zacharia ran her first press briefing on Tuesday which ran for 14 minutes where she took three questions from reporters and dropped the news about the resignation of U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle.

Zacharia lasted just five days in the role.

data.title: Watch live: 'The Morning Meeting' breaks down key midterm races
data.description:
With control of Congress on the line, 2WAY is teaming up with NewsNation and The Hill for a special edition of “The Morning Meeting” ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

The program will take a closer look at key House and Senate races as Republicans and Democrats make their final pitches to voters.

2WAY’s Mark Halperin, Larry O’Connor and Kevin Walling will host the discussion, joined by NewsNation anchor Leland Vittert, The Hill’s Amie Parnes and reporters from Nexstar stations across the country.

data.title: Loomer lobbies to replace Zacharia: 'Hear me out'
data.description:
Far-right activist Laura Loomer put herself forward as a candidate for White House press secretary as Katie Zacharia was ousted from the role after just five days on Friday. 

In three separate posts on the social media platform X, the conservative influencer argued her case.

“Here me out: Press Secretary Laura Loomer,” she wrote in an initial post. 

Two hours later, Loomer followed up by stating she would “be an amazing Press Secretary.”

“I’d show President Trump all the receipts,” she continued. “I would bring my binder full of receipts to every briefing.”

Loomer also posted an image of her face poorly cropped onto an image of a woman with long blonde hair. Both Zacharia and former press secretary Karoline Leavitt are blonde.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment on Loomer’s posts.

Zacharia faced criticism after she cut short her first press briefing Tuesday, appearing visibly nervous and only taking three questions from White House reporters. Additionally, questions regarding her legal background have garnered scrutiny this week.

Loomer defended Zacharia in a Friday X post, accusing critics of being “unnecessarily cruel.”

“I wish Katie the best,” Loomer wrote. “I think it’s great that President Trump has people who are so devoted to his cause they are willing to subject themselves to public nitpicking on a daily basis. I’m sure he appreciates it and I think Katie had good intentions.”

Prior to Zacharia’s appointment as press secretary, several Trump allies were floated as possible contenders to replace Leavitt, including White House deputy press secretary Anna Kelly, former acting U.S. Attorney for New Jersey Alina Habba, former Department of Homeland Security Assistant Secretary Tricia McLaughlin and conservative commentator Scott Jennings.

On Friday, prediction market Kalshi had Jennings as the top contender to fill this role, followed by Kelly and conservative author Elizabeth Pipko.

Trump told Fox News’s senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy following the news of Zacharia’s departure on Friday that he was not in a rush to fill the vacancy.

data.title: Trump to campaign in Michigan
data.description:
President Trump will campaign in Michigan next week, marking what is slated to be his seventh campaign stop in a seven-day stretch.

The Republican National Committee said Friday Trump will headline a rally in St. Clair County, Mich. on Sunday, Oct. 25 following an appearance in Macon, Ga. the day prior.

Trump’s midterm travel schedule is packed next week. On Monday, he will rally Republicans in Wichita, Kansas before heading to Greenville, N.C. Tuesday. The president will then campaign in Clemson, S.C. on Wednesday, Sioux City, Iowa on Thursday and Fort Myers, Fla. on Friday. 

Michigan is home to highly competitive gubernatorial, Senate and House races. The state’s Senate race has been in the national spotlight, with many Democrats saying they are growing increasingly optimistic about Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s chances of winning. 

Progressive Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) campaigned with El-Sayed in the Wolverine State this week, and former President Obama is set to campaign there on Oct. 24 — a day before Trump’s visit.

Vice President Vance campaigned with Republican Senate nominee and former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) on Thursday. 

While Rogers has appeared with Trump on the campaign trail in Michigan, he has made an effort to distance himself from some of the president’s policies — including his tariffs and trade war with Canada.

data.title: Unauthorized drones banned along US-Mexico border: FAA
data.description:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said Friday it is restricting unauthorized drones along the ​U.S.-Mexico border.

This move comes as the government ramps up efforts to address concerns about illegal drug shipment across the border, Reuters reported Friday.

It is a temporary flight restriction that bars any unauthorized drone activity up to 400 feet above ground and extends 1 nautical mile north of the U.S.-Mexico border, the report said.

In February, the FAA temporarily closed the airspace over El Paso, Texas, and southern New Mexico as a result of the Pentagon’s plan to test antidrone technology. The order was lifted hours later.

Later in August, the U.S. military used a high-energy laser to shoot down three drones near the southern border that officials said were linked to Mexican drug cartels. This operation involved the Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser system to bring down the drones along the U.S.-Mexican border.

Customs and Boder Protection sources said the following month that the number of suspected cartel-linked drones in the Rio Grande Valley region of Texas along the U.S.-Mexico border has dropped by 75 percent since the military started using the high-energy lasers.

Officials, however, acknowledged that the drop in the number could be due to the cartel changing routes or using other tactics to achieve the goal of surveilling U.S. activity.

The FAA’s drone sighting report says the administration receives more than 100 reports of sightings each month from law enforcement, pilots and citizens. Between July and September, more than 500 sightings were reported, according to FAA data.

data.title: Rep. Andy Harris on spat with student reporter: 'I pushed back, liberal media got offended'
data.description:
Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.) is defending himself after video of him clashing with a student reporter during a press gaggle went viral earlier this week.

In an appearance on Fox 45 Baltimore Thursday, anchor Mikenzie Frost asked Harris about the moment and pressed him on if he regretted the exchange.

“It’s not very newsworthy that the liberal media badgers a conservative politician, what was newsworthy is that I actually pushed back against it,” Harris said. “She actually started by criticizing the way that press gaggle was being conducted. That’s not the role of a journalist.”

The video, which the Baltimore Banner posted to social platform X Wednesday, shows Harris asking Capital News Service reporter Cat Murphy to stop recording the press gaggle, claiming she needed permission to do so under Maryland’s two-party consent law before appearing to threaten her with legal action.

However, the law Harris cited does not apply to public situations with “no reasonable expectation of privacy.”

Another video angle, shared by the Baltimore Sun on X, shows Murphy telling Harris to “respect their questions just as much as mine,” though it is not clear in the video what prompted the comment. Harris responded by saying he would not answer her questions.

Harris appeared to reference this moment during his Thursday interview, telling Frost that the reporter had been “telling me how to conduct the press conference” — which he also said is not the “purpose” of a journalist in this setting.

In an appearance on CNN, Murphy told anchor Jake Tapper the incident has been “a lot” to take in.

“It has been a lot. But I was focused on doing my job and asking my questions that I wanted answers to, and I think I did that,” Murphy said.

In Harris’ Fox 45 interview, Frost pointed out that Harris threatened to bring in police and have Murphy prosecuted for recording him, prompting the GOP lawmaker to reiterate his argument that Murphy was violating the two-party consent law during the interaction.

Harris went on to repeatedly blame “the liberal media” for the incident and subsequent social media firestorm. The GOP lawmaker is the current chair and an original member of the House Freedom Caucus, which includes some of the most conservative members of Congress.

“The liberal media has been doing this for years. Nobody pushes back. I pushed back, liberal media got offended,” Harris said.

The gaggle in question occurred after Harris wrapped up a debate against his opponent, Democrat Dan Schwartz, in the race for Maryland’s 1st Congressional District. Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ gives Harris, the incumbent, a 95 percent chance of victory in November.

data.title: Voto Latino reveals six-figure Texas investment alongside Talarico, Hinojosa event
data.description:
Voto Latino on Friday unveiled a new six-figure investment aimed at boosting Latino voter engagement in Texas with early voting kicking off in the state next week. 

The civic engagement organization said in a news release first shared with The Hill that it was investing over $500,000 in the state. The investment comes ahead of the group’s event in the Rio Grande Valley later this month with Democratic candidates running in closely-watched midterm races. 

President Trump and Republicans seen his support among Latino voters slip heading into the November elections, in which he has repeatedly urged Americans to cast their votes as if he were “on the ballot.” This voting demographic was key to the president’s 2024 victory in the state.

Maria Teresa Kumar, the group’s president and co-founder, called Texas “ground zero for change” in a statement announcing this investment.

“We are heading straight to the epicenter of the Latino vote to make sure every voter is ready to cast their ballot,” Kumar said. “Latinos are on the brink of changing the political landscape of Texas and the nation.”

The group’s Oct. 25 event will feature three Democratic candidates in tightly-contested midterm races, including gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa, Senate hopeful James Talarico and House candidate Bobby Pulido. 

Hinojosa, who is running to unseat Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), said there was “no better place” to close out her campaign. 

“For too long, Texans have been paying more and getting less under Greg Abbott,” she said in a statement. “I’m proud to be joining Voto Latino, making sure every family in the Valley has the information and the power to make their voice heard from now until Election Day.” 

Talarico is running in a tightly-contested race against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R).

“Latino families in Texas have always carried this state forward, and they should have leaders who listen and deliver,” he said in a statement. “Our democracy works best when every neighbor has a seat at the table, and I’m grateful to Voto Latino for bringing us together for these final days.”

Pulido, a Latin Grammy-winning singer from the Rio Grande Valley, is running in the state’s 15th District against incumbent GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz.

“What I hear from families isn’t about left or right. They want good jobs, affordable health care, and schools that give their kids a real shot,” he said in a statement. “Our community has always shown up for one another, and I’m proud to be here with Voto Latino to make sure every voice in the Valley is heard.”
